docs.title: Confusion Matrix
docs.text:
Actual Yes Actual No Predicted Yes True Positive False Positive Predicted No False Negative True Negative - TP : Caught the thing correctly - FP : False Alarm - FN : Missed It - TN : Correctly Ignored it ## Accuracy

[!tip] Accuracy refers to "out of everything I predicted, how many did i get right" - This includes how much true positives and how much true negatives we caught

\[Accuracy = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}\]

[!warning] This fails when the data is unbalanced - If positive cases make 99% of the data, then predicting everything as positive gives us a 99% accuracy which is not good

docs.title: Precision
docs.text:
[!tip] Precision refers to "of all the predicted positives, how many are actual positives" - It is the number of true positives among the predicted positives

\[Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\]

docs.title: Recall (Sensitivity)
docs.text:
[!tip] Recall refers to "of all the actual positives, how many did I successfully find" - It is the number of true positives among the total number of actual positive cases

\[Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\]

docs.title: Specificity
docs.text:
[!tip] Specificity is the opposite of Recall - It refers to "of all the actual negatives, how many did I correctly ignore"

\[Specificity = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}\]

docs.title: F1-Measure
docs.text:
[!tip] If we care about both precision and recall, use F1. - It is low when either of precision or recall is low - It is high when both are high - It is the Harmonic Mean of precision and recall

\[\text{F1-Measure} = \frac{2 \times Precision \times Recall}{Precision + Recall}\]

docs.title: Question 1: Evaluation of Cancer Detection ML System
docs.text:
1.1 Given - Total population = 100,000 - Actual cancer patients (positive class) = 400 - Healthy individuals (negative class) = 99,600 - Correctly identified cancer patients = 100 - Healthy individuals incorrectly flagged as cancer = 200 - Total wrong predictions = 500

  1. TP -> Correct Prediction + Predicted as has Cancer => Patients who have cancer and predicted as has cancer. => 100
  2. FP -> Incorrect Prediction + Predicted as has Cancer => Patients who are healthy and predicted as has cancer. => 200
  3. TN -> Correct Prediction + Predicted as has no Cancer => Patients who are healthy and predicted as healthy. => 100,000 - 400 - 200 = 99,400
  4. FN -> Incorrect Prediction + Predicted as has no Cancer => Patients who has cancer but predicted as has no cancer. => 300

1.2. Clinically more dangerous error

False Negatives are more dangerous than False Positives.

Justification:

  • A false negative means cancer is not detected, which can delay diagnosis and treatment.
  • Delayed treatment in cancer can significantly reduce survival rates.
  • False positives cause stress and additional tests, but usually do not threaten life directly.

1.3. $\(Accuracy = \frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}\)$ $\(Accuracy = \frac{100+99,400}{100+200+99,400+300}=99.5\%\)$

  • Why deceptively high? Because the dataset is highly imbalanced. Even if the model predicted everyone was "Healthy," it would still achieve 99.6% accuracy

1.4. $\(Precision = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} = \frac{100}{100 + 200} = 33.3\%\)$ - Only 1/3 of people flagged with cancer actually have it. Trustworthiness is low

1.5. $\(Recall = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} = \frac{100}{100+300} = 25\%\)$ - The system misses 75% of actual cancer cases, making it very ineffective for screening

1.6. - Accuracy is high because it is dominated by the massive number of True Negatives (healthy people). Recall is low because the model fails to identify the majority of the small "positive" class

1.7. - Recall is the most useful metric here. In medical screening, the priority is to ensure no actual cases are missed (minimizing False Negatives), even if it means more follow-up tests for False Positives

1.8. - Benefit: The F1-score provides a single harmonic mean of Precision and Recall, penalizing the model for having a very low value in either. - Insufficiency: F1 treats Precision and Recall as equally important. In this clinical case, Recall is far more critical than Precision, so F1 might still mask a dangerously low Recall rate

docs.title: Question 2: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
docs.text:
2.1 - Query point: Q = (3, 3) - Distance metric: Squared Euclidean Distance

Point ID x y Class Distance Calculation \(d^2\) A1 1 1 A \((3-1)^2 + (3-1)^2\) 8 A2 1 3 A \((3-1)^2 + (3-3)^2\) 4 A3 2 2 A \((3-2)^2 + (3-2)^2\) 2 B1 4 4 B \((3-4)^2 + (3-4)^2\) 2 B2 5 4 B \((3-5)^2 + (3-4)^2\) 5 B3 4 5 B \((3-4)^2 + (3-5)^2\) 5

2.2. - when k = 1 - Nearest points are A3 or B1 - Votes for A = 1 - Votes for B = 1 - There is a tie, so we choose the first one => A - Prediction = A (tie breaked) - when k = 3 - Nearest points are A3, B1, A2 - Votes for A = 2 - Votes for B = 1 - Prediction = A - when k = 5 - Nearest points are A3, B1, A2, B2, B3 - Votes for A = 2 - Votes for B = 3 - Prediction = B

2.3. - A very large k includes points that are far away and likely belong to different clusters. This ignores the local structure of the data and makes the decision boundary too smooth, essentially predicting the majority class of the entire dataset regardless of where the query point is located.

2.4. k = 1 is more affected.

  • Why: k = 1 makes its decision based solely on the single nearest neighbor. If that one point is mislabeled, the prediction will be 100% wrong. k = 5 is more robust because it averages the votes of 5 points, so one bad point is less likely to flip the final result.

2.5. - a) Greatest Contributor: The neighbors with the smallest distance (A3 and B1) contribute the most. - b) Reducing Ties: Yes. Weighted voting makes it much rarer for the sums of weights to be exactly equal, as it accounts for the precise proximity of each point rather than just a simple count.

docs.title: Logistic Regression, Regularization and Bias Variance
1. The Bias-Variance Shift
docs.text:
By applying heavy L2 regularization, you essentially traded High Variance for High Bias.

  • Initial State: The model was over-complex (High Variance), memorizing the training data perfectly but failing to generalize to new patients.
  • The Shift: The L2 penalty reduced model complexity by shrinking the weights. However, the penalty was too "heavy," pushing the model past the sweet spot into underfitting (High Bias). It became too simple to see the patterns of the rare disease.

docs.title: 2. The Sigmoid "Flattening"
docs.text:
The sigmoid function is defined as:

$$ \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(wx + b)}} $$ - Flattening: When L2 forces weights (\(w\)) to be very small, the input \(z\) stays near zero. This creates a flatter, less responsive curve rather than a sharp "S" shape. - The Problem: A flatter curve means the model is less sensitive to changes in patient data. Because the disease is so rare, a flat curve makes it nearly impossible for the output probability to "climb" high enough to cross the 0.5 threshold to predict "Sick."

docs.title: 3. The Accuracy Paradox
docs.text:
In a dataset where 99.5% of people are healthy, accuracy is a trap.

  • The Default Score: If your model simply predicts "Healthy" for every single person, it achieves 99.5% accuracy while doing zero actual work.
  • Why it's useless: A doctor doesn't need a model to tell them a healthy person is healthy; they need it to find the needle in the haystack. By "improving" accuracy, you likely just trained the model to ignore the 0.5% of sick patients to avoid the risk of being "wrong" on the majority.

docs.title: 4. Critical Decision
docs.text:
I would choose Model A.

  • Clinical Priorities: In medicine, a False Negative (missing a sick patient) is far more dangerous than a False Positive (a "scare" for a healthy person).
  • The Choice: Model A has a high Recall, catching 95% of cases. Even though it "over-diagnoses" (False Positives), those patients can be cleared with follow-up testing. Model B is "accurate" but lethal, as it leaves 90% of sick patients untreated (False Negatives).

docs.title: Adapter
docs.text:
• Is a Structural Design Pattern
  • Also known as wrapper pattern
  • An adapter allows incompatible interfaces to work together
  • It converts one interface into another that the client expects
Role Meaning Client Existing code that expects some interface Target The interface the client expects Adaptee Existing / new / legacy class with incompatible interface Adapter The translator between Target and Adaptee >Adapter adapts the adaptee to the target interface
  • Client knows only Target
  • Adapter implements Target
  • Adapter internally calls Adaptee
  • Client thinks it's talking to Target

docs.title: Object Adapter
docs.text:
• Adapter has an instance of Adaptee
  • Adapter delegates to the adaptee instance
interface Target {
    void request();
}

class Adaptee {
    public void specificRequest() {
        System.out.println("Specific Request");
    }
}

class ObjectAdapter implements Target {
    private Adaptee adaptee;

    public ObjectAdapter(Adaptee adaptee) {
        this.adaptee = adaptee;
    }

    @Override
    public void request() {
        adaptee.specificRequest();
    }
}

class Client {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Adaptee adaptee = new Adaptee();
        Target target = new ObjectAdapter(adaptee);

        target.request();
    }
}

docs.text:
• Adapter is-a Adaptee
  • Adapter pretends to be Target
class ClassAdapter extends Adapter implements Target {
    @Override
    public void request() {
        specificRequest();
    }
}

class Client {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Target target = new ClassAdapter();

        target.request();

docs.title: Facade
docs.text:
• Is a Structural Design Pattern
  • Facade provides a simple, unified interface to a complex subsystem
  • It hides the complexity and gives you a single easy entry point
  • Create one class that:
    • Knows the subsystem
    • Coordinates the calls
    • Exposes a simple API

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• Subsystem is complex
  • Client code is messy
  • For loose coupling
  • To expose a clean API
Engine engine = new Engine();
engine.start();

FuelInjector injector = new FuelInjector();
injector.inject();

AirFlowController air = new AirFlowController();
air.control();

CarStarter starter = new CarStarter();
starter.start();

class CarFacade {
    private Engine engine = new Engine();
    private FuelInjector injector = new FuelInjector();
    private AirFlowController airFlow = new AirFlowController();

    void startCar() {
        engine.start();
        injector.inject();
        airFlow.control();
        System.out.println("Car started");
    }
}

public class Client {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        CarFacade car = new CarFacade();
        car.startCar();
    }
}

docs.title: Observer
docs.text:
• Is a behavioral pattern
  • Observer defines a one to many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically
  • One object publishes changes, many objects react

docs.title: Solves
docs.text:
• Tight coupling
  • Need to explicitly know who all to notify
  • Adding / Removing listeners difficulty
Role Responsibility Subject Maintains list of observers ConcreteSubject Holds state Observer Interface for notification ConcreteObserver Reacts to changes 
interface Observer {
    void update(int temperature);
}

interface Subject {
    void registerObserver(Observer o);
    void removeObserver(Observer o);
    void notifyObservers();
}

class WeatherStation implements Subject {
    private List<Observer> observers = new ArrayList<>();
    private int temperature;

    public void setTemperature(int temp) {
        this.temperature = temp;
        notifyObservers();
    }

    @Override
    public void registerObserver(Observer o) {
        this.observers.add(o);
    }

    @Override
    public void removeObserver(Observer o) {
        this.observers.remove(o);
    }

    @Override
    public void notifyObservers() {
        for (Observer o : observers) {
            o.update(temperature);
        }
    }
}

class PhoneDisplay implements Observer {
    @Override
    public void update(int temperature) {
        System.out.println("updated temp in phone display");
    }
}

class TVDisplay implements Observer {
    @Override
    public void update(int temperature) {
        System.out.println("updated temp in TV display");
    }
}

class Client {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        WeatherStation station = new WeatherStation();
        Observer phone = new PhoneDisplay();
        Observer tv = new TVDisplay();

        station.registerObserver(phone);
        station.registerObserver(tv);

        station.setTemperature(10);
        station.setTemperature(20);
    }
}
  • There will be two interfaces corresponding to
    • Observer
    • Subject
  • And two or more implementations for the same

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Subject keep track of the observers
  • When generates the events
    • It loops through the observers
    • notify each of the observers
  • We can keep a get and set state methods in the concrete implementation of subject if the observers need to get some data from the subject on notification

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
• Iterative changes to the software
  • First version of the software is developed after which reviews are considered, and changes are made to make another iteration.
  • If everything goes well, the product is deployed.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
• When the requirements are known.
  • When there are changes to requirements in future.
  • When the software is large.
  • A new technology is present and is learnt by the development team while developing
  • When there are high risk features present that have to be reviewed in future.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
• Testing and debugging during smaller iteration is easy.
  • More time can be spend on designing and planning than documentation.
  • It easily accepts changes to the software after the initial iterations.
  • Risks are identified and can be changed in the next iteration.
  • There is a parallel planning team to review changes for the next iteration.

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
• It is not suitable for smaller projects.
  • More resources are required.
  • Project completion cannot be decided.
  • Requirement changes can have an affect to the budget.
  • More time consumed due to design changes in later iterations.

• In this model, a prototype of the original software is created.

docs.text:
• Prototype model does not have to know complete details about input, output and processes.

  • Flexible, can accommodate changes.
  • Errors can be detected easily.
  • Helps team member to communicate easily and understand specifications.

• Client involvement is more
  • It is a very slow process
  • Many changes can disturb the rhythm
  • Documentation is very poor due to constant changes
  • Costly in terms of time and money.
  • Prototyping tools are expensive.

docs.title: Aggregation
docs.text:
• "Is part of" relationship
  • Represents a whole part relationship
  • Represented by a diamond symbol
  • If parent is destroyed, child still lives

example: - Library has Books - Books can exist outside the library - Team has Players - Players can exist even if the team is disbanded

  • Symbol is hollow diamond in the parent side

docs.title: Association
docs.text:
• "knows a" relationship
  • allows communication between objects using its id (pointer)
  • Can be 1-1, 1-n, n-1, etc
  • Represented by a straight labelled line

docs.title: Association and Link
docs.text:
• An association is a class level relationship
  • Link is an object level relationship

docs.title: example:
docs.text:
• A Teacher teaches a student = Association
  • "Kiran" teaches "Alvin" = Link

docs.title: Qualified Association
docs.text:
• A qualified association is an association where you use a key (qualifier) to uniquely select one (or a subset of) related objects
  • Association + Lookup Key
  • Like ISBN of a book instead of the pointer to the book
  • We keep a map of qualifiers to pointers for lookup
  • Use of qualifier changes the cardinality

example: Library --- Book (0..*) Library --- [ISBN] --- Book (0..1)

Association comes when: - A delegates to B - A needs help from B - A and B are peers

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
• "is made of" relationship
  • One class owns another completely
  • If parent is destroyed, child must die

example: - House has rooms - Room cannot exist without a house - Human's has heart - Heart belongs to that human completely

  • Symbol is filled diamond in the parent side

Composition comes where: - B is a permanent part of A - A contains B - A is a permanent collection of Bs

docs.title: Dependency
docs.text:
• One class uses another class temporarily
  • No field, no ownership
  • Short lived
  • Once task is done, relationship is gone
class Printer {
    void print() {}
}

class Report {
    void generate(Printer printer) {
        printer.print();
    }
}
  • Symbol is dotted arrow from dependent to independent class
  • Report - - - > Printer

docs.title: Inheritance
docs.text:
• "has a " relationship
  • Car is a Vehicle
  • Human is an Animal
  • Represented by an arrow towards the parent

docs.title: Discriminators
docs.text:
• Can be used to separate child classes into clusters
  • Here issuable and reference are discriminators

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:

  • Overuse can result in poor quality of code

Inheritance comes where: - A is a kind of B - A is a specialization of B - A behaves like B
